about: Story tree facts R4 to R9 for the talk 'The ultimate insider' (Dinis Cruz), researched 2026-10-29 by a research agent for researcher@the-ultimate-insider. Captures in work/captures/story-* (plus reused fig-dbir-2026-pdf, verizon-dbir-2025, anthropic-espionage-news).

r4.answer: Mostly yes, with a near miss: GTIG (Sept 2026) says it 'has not yet observed' fully autonomous AI pipelines used against targets in the wild, and NCSC judges fully automated end-to-end attacks unlikely to 2027; but GTIG (May 2026) found a criminal AI-built zero-day 'planned' for a mass exploitation event that it may have prevented, and Anthropic (Nov 2025) reported a largely AI-run espionage campaign against about thirty targets. Say 'not yet observed at scale', not 'not happening'.

items.what: GTIG has not seen fully autonomous pipelines in the wild
items.quote: While recent model security incident disclosures demonstrate that frontier models can autonomously identify zero-days and execute network intrusions, GTIG has not yet observed threat actors deploying fully autonomous pipelines against targets in the wild.

items.what: Same report: agentic frameworks already used at scale for scanning and credential harvesting (counterweight)
items.quote: Adversaries are deploying multi-agent frameworks that autonomously manage scanning pipelines, resolve operational errors, and execute credential harvesting at scale.

items.what: First AI-developed zero-day seen; mass exploitation planned, possibly prevented (counter-evidence)
items.quote: The criminal threat actor planned to use it in a mass exploitation event but our proactive counter discovery may have prevented its use.

items.what: NCSC: fully automated end-to-end attacks unlikely to 2027
items.quote: The development of fully automated, end-to-end advanced cyber attacks is unlikely to 2027.

items.what: DBIR 2026: AI-assisted malware mostly reuses known techniques
items.quote: Most AI-assisted development of malware and tooling was associated with well-known and defined attack techniques, with a median of 55 existing known malware examples performing the same functions.

items.what: Anthropic: AI ran 80-90% of an espionage campaign, about 30 targets (counter-evidence, targeted not mass)
items.quote: Overall, the threat actor was able to use AI to perform 80-90% of the campaign, with human intervention required only sporadically

items.what: GTIG Nov 2025: no breakthrough capabilities seen in IO use
items.quote: For observed IO campaigns, we did not see evidence of successful automation or any breakthrough capabilities.

r4.not_found: OpenAI threat reports, Anthropic 2026 threat reports and Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2025/2026 were not captured in the time box.

r5.answer: The data found says the opposite on initial access: exploitation of vulnerabilities is rising, not falling, as an entry route (DBIR 20% to 31% of breaches; edge devices and VPNs 3% to 22% of exploitation targets; Mandiant: exploits top vector six years running at 32%). No Shodan or Censys multi-year exposure trend was captured, so 'smaller surface' is unsupported; 'more mature' is not what breach data shows.

items.what: DBIR 2026: exploitation is now the top initial access vector, 31% up from 20%
items.quote: The exploitation of vulnerabilities is the most prominent initial access vector in our dataset this year, reaching the height of 31%, up from 20% last year, which represents a 55% increase in this vector.

items.what: DBIR 2025: edge devices and VPNs 22% of exploitation targets, up from 3%
items.quote: The percentage of edge devices and VPNs as a target on our exploitation of vulnerabilities action was 22%, and it grew almost eight-fold12 from the 3% found in last year's report.

items.what: DBIR 2026: unpatched edge devices behind 29% of opportunistic victimisation (subset context)
items.quote: unpatched vulnerabilities in edge devices (29%) that resulted in them being victimized

items.what: M-Trends 2026: exploits top initial infection vector, sixth year, 32%
items.quote: Exploits remained the most common initial infection vector for the sixth consecutive year, accounting for 32% of intrusions.

r5.not_found: A multi-year Shodan or Censys count of exposed services (any direction) was not looked up in the time box; no source found supporting 'smaller and more mature'.

r6.answer: GAO (July 2025) found 11 critical federal legacy systems 23 to 60 years old costing about $754 million a year, 8 of 11 in outdated languages and 7 with known vulnerabilities, with about 80% of $100B+ federal IT spend going to operations and maintenance. The '800 billion lines of COBOL' figure is a 2022 vendor-commissioned survey; the much repeated Reuters 2017 figures (220 billion lines, 43% of banking systems, 95% of ATM swipes) were not captured.

items.what: GAO: 11 critical legacy systems, age and cost
items.quote: According to the agencies, these 11 systems ranged from about 23 to 60 years old and collectively cost approximately $754 million annually to operate and maintain.

items.what: GAO: outdated languages, unsupported parts, known vulnerabilities
items.quote: Eight of the 11 systems use outdated languages, four have unsupported hardware or software, and seven are operating with known cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

items.what: GAO: Treasury systems on COBOL and Assembly, dwindling skills
items.quote: both of the Department of the Treasury's selected systems run on Common Business Oriented Language (COBOL) and Assembly Language Code, programming languages that have a dwindling number of people available with the skills needed to support them.

items.what: GAO: about 80% of federal IT spend on operations and maintenance
items.quote: Of this amount, agencies have typically reported spending about 80 percent on operations and maintenance of existing IT.

items.what: Micro Focus / Vanson Bourne survey: 775 to 850 billion lines of COBOL in daily use (vendor-commissioned estimate)
items.quote: According to the global survey, the amount of COBOL code in daily use increased significantly to 775-850 billion lines.

r6.not_found: Reuters 2017 COBOL graphic is JS-rendered (capture partial, figures not carried). No regulator figure on share of transactions running on COBOL found; GAO quote describes systems maintained at cost, not 'unmaintained' code, so 'nobody maintains' is a stretch: say 'few can maintain'.

r7.answer: ux.sgit.ai (v0.4.1, last checked 2026-10-25) documents, for the Claude iOS app, a permission prompt that asks for a security decision with only truncated raw code (UX-059, high), plus voice controls where one unlabelled X discards a recording (UX-060, high) and the 'send as is' button sits unlabelled next to 'stop and edit' (UX-061, medium). These are the author's own first-hand findings on one product.

items.what: Claude app permission prompt: approve code it does not explain, cut off
items.quote: The person is asked to make a security decision and given only code to make it with, partly hidden, on a phone. In practice the choice is to stop the work or to trust blindly, and every prompt like this teaches the habit of pressing Allow without reading

items.what: Unlabelled 'send as is' next to 'stop and edit': uncorrected text sent to an agent that acts on it
items.quote: a wrong tap either destroys the recording (UX-060) or sends a message full of transcription errors to an agent that will act on it.

items.what: One unlabelled X discards a recording with no confirmation or undo
items.quote: The X discards the recording and its transcript at once: no "discard this recording?", no undo, no copy kept.

r7.not_found: The register has no findings yet for other frontier tools (e.g. ChatGPT, Cursor, Claude Code CLI); the three are all one product (Claude app on iPhone/iPad), observed by the author.

r8.answer: Vendor-reported, via secondary news: Lovable says users created more than 60 million projects since November 2024, with Lovable-built apps getting 900 million visits a month (Aug 2026); Replit reported over 50 million registered users at its March 2026 Series D. Neither figure separates non-developers; all are vendor claims relayed by press.

items.what: Lovable: 60M+ projects since Nov 2024, 900M monthly visits (vendor-reported)
items.quote: The company said users have created more than 60 million projects since its launch in November 2024, while Lovable-built applications receive more than 900 million visits each month.

items.what: Replit: over 50 million registered users (vendor-reported)
items.quote: The total number of registered users is over 50 million.

r8.not_found: No primary vendor post captured (Lovable and Replit blogs not found in the time box; replit.com/blog/series-d is 404). No figures captured for Bolt, Vercel v0 or Cursor, and no analyst count of apps built by non-developers. Search snippets (not captured) attribute ~100k new Lovable projects a day and 'most of 60 million Replit users are not professional programmers'; treat as unverified.

r9.answer: Dinis Cruz uses the terms in a family of 'behaviour policies' (agents, decisions, workflows, skills, applications, processes). A process behaviour policy is derived from one traced run (every file, syscall, host) and enforced by the Linux kernel; a decision policy ('Agent Decision Policy') says at a branch point who chooses, on what evidence, within what limits, and who is called when out of bounds. The exact phrase 'decision behaviour policy' was not found: his term is 'decision policy'.

items.what: The behaviour policy family
items.quote: The behaviour policy family has policies for agents, decisions, workflows, skills and applications. This one is for a process.

items.what: Process behaviour policy: derived from a traced run
items.quote: A policy is derived from one traced run: every file the process reads, every system call it makes, every host it talks to. Then the kernel enforces it with seven walls

items.what: The policy executes nothing; the kernel enforces it
items.quote: The policy is derived, not written.** One traced run lists every file, system call and host the process needs. - **The kernel enforces it.** Seven walls, set from the policy; the policy itself executes nothing.

items.what: Agent Decision Policy definition
items.quote: An Agent Decision Policy says, at a branch point, who chooses, on what evidence, within what limits, and who to call when it is out of bounds.

items.what: Why 'decision'
items.quote: The word "decision" matters because it is the one the business and the risk team already use.

items.what: Decision policy for an application
items.quote: **The decision policy** says who decides what. Who may accept the blast radius of each row that stays open; who decides the site comes back

r9.not_found: The exact phrase 'decision behaviour policy' does not occur in the captured llms.txt files of newsroom.sgit.ai, sgit.ai, riskmandate.ai, abp.sgit.ai or newsroom llms-full.txt; nothing found outside his own sites (not searched widely). Publication dates of three-policies and application-behaviour-policies not extracted.

claims.text: AI-driven mass exploitation has not been observed yet

evidence.quote: While recent model security incident disclosures demonstrate that frontier models can autonomously identify zero-days and execute network intrusions, GTIG has not yet observed threat actors deploying fully autonomous pipelines against targets in the wild.
The development of fully automated, end-to-end advanced cyber attacks is unlikely to 2027.
The criminal threat actor planned to use it in a mass exploitation event but our proactive counter discovery may have prevented its use.
Overall, the threat actor was able to use AI to perform 80-90% of the campaign, with human intervention required only sporadically
Adversaries are deploying multi-agent frameworks that autonomously manage scanning pipelines, resolve operational errors, and execute credential harvesting at scale.

claims.note: Disputed in detail, so capped at A2: GTIG says no fully autonomous pipelines seen in the wild, but it also caught an AI-built zero-day planned for mass exploitation (May 2026) and reports agentic credential harvesting at scale.
claims.suggested_wording: Threat intelligence has not yet seen fully autonomous AI attacks in the wild; the first AI-built zero-day meant for mass exploitation was caught in May 2026.

claims.text: the internet-facing surface is smaller and more mature than it was

evidence.quote: The exploitation of vulnerabilities is the most prominent initial access vector in our dataset this year, reaching the height of 31%, up from 20% last year, which represents a 55% increase in this vector.
The percentage of edge devices and VPNs as a target on our exploitation of vulnerabilities action was 22%, and it grew almost eight-fold12 from the 3% found in last year's report.
Exploits remained the most common initial infection vector for the sixth consecutive year, accounting for 32% of intrusions.

claims.note: No exposure-trend source found for 'smaller'. Breach data shows exploitation of internet-facing systems, especially edge devices, rising as the way in.
claims.suggested_wording: Exploiting internet-facing systems is now the top way in (31% of breaches in DBIR 2026, up from 20%), so the old surface is not shrinking in the data, while the new insider surface grows beside it.

claims.text: legacy code doing mission-critical work that nobody maintains

evidence.quote: According to the agencies, these 11 systems ranged from about 23 to 60 years old and collectively cost approximately $754 million annually to operate and maintain.

both of the Department of the Treasury's selected systems run on Common Business Oriented Language (COBOL) and Assembly Language Code, programming languages that have a dwindling number of people available with the skills needed to support them.
According to the global survey, the amount of COBOL code in daily use increased significantly to 775-850 billion lines.

claims.note: GAO is the primary record for the federal systems (A6); they are maintained at high cost by a dwindling pool, not unmaintained. The 800 billion lines of COBOL is a 2022 vendor survey (A1).
claims.suggested_wording: Decades-old code that few people can still maintain: GAO's 11 most critical US federal legacy systems are 23 to 60 years old and cost $754 million a year to run.

claims.text: bad security usability in frontier tools (ux.sgit.ai examples)

evidence.quote: The person is asked to make a security decision and given only code to make it with, partly hidden, on a phone. In practice the choice is to stop the work or to trust blindly, and every prompt like this teaches the habit of pressing Allow without reading
a wrong tap either destroys the recording (UX-060) or sends a message full of transcription errors to an agent that will act on it.
The X discards the recording and its transcript at once: no "discard this recording?", no undo, no copy kept.

claims.note: Author's own findings, one product (Claude app iOS), last checked 2026-10-25.

claims.text: volume of new applications built by non-developers with AI tools

evidence.quote: The company said users have created more than 60 million projects since its launch in November 2024, while Lovable-built applications receive more than 900 million visits each month.
The total number of registered users is over 50 million.

claims.note: Vendor-reported via press; counts projects and users, not non-developer apps in production.
claims.suggested_wording: Lovable alone reports more than 60 million projects since November 2024 (vendor figure).

claims.text: process behaviour policies and decision behaviour policies

evidence.quote: A policy is derived from one traced run: every file the process reads, every system call it makes, every host it talks to. Then the kernel enforces it with seven walls
An Agent Decision Policy says, at a branch point, who chooses, on what evidence, within what limits, and who to call when it is out of bounds.

claims.note: His published term is 'decision policy' (Agent Decision Policy), part of the behaviour policy family; 'decision behaviour policy' not found verbatim.
